title: The 2025 price increase
question: What did the 2025 price increase do to sessions and revenue?
answer: It cost between 1% and 10% of sessions at the raised sites, and raised their revenue by 7% to 18%.
decision: Keep the higher price. Revenue rises at every effect size the data allows, so the decision does not depend on the exact number.
rests_on: 290 raised sites against 408 unchanged ones over two years of weekly data.
The usual comparisons say sessions went up (+4.1% before and after, +1.5% with two-way fixed effects): the raised sites were growing faster.
The weeks before each increase show it: the raised sites pulled ahead by 0.18% a week before anything changed (p = 1e-08).

Two methods that allow for that disagree in a known direction: controls reweighted to grow like the raised sites (synthetic DiD) give the smaller loss, each site's own growth continued (trend imputation) the larger one.
would_change: A randomised price test, which would narrow the range to a single number (question 2 shows how).
Evidence that growth at the raised sites was about to slow sharply, which would move the answer towards the smaller loss.
method: Before/after, two-way fixed effects, imputation (Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess), event study, synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al.), capacity-aware trend imputation; site bootstrap.

title: The night discount trial
question: Should the night discount go network-wide?
answer: The 30% night discount moves 4.2 points of energy to the night and cuts daytime sessions by 6%, but costs €143 of revenue per site and day.

number.label: net value per site and day

decision: Do not roll it out at 30%. The relieved daytime demand is worth less than the revenue it gives away; test a smaller discount on the busiest sites only.
rests_on: 80 sites, 4480 site-days, discount assigned by coin flip each day (randomisation p = 0.002).
Designed from pre-trial data: the trial could detect €32 a day (1.5% of revenue) with 80% power.
Yesterday's discount still shifts a little charging today (0.4 points), so the model separates the two.
An always-valid sequential test would have stopped the trial on day 7.
would_change: A higher value of a relieved daytime session than €4 (grid peak charges, queues), which would have to exceed about €31 to pay.
method: Switchback design by site and day; fixed effects for site and date with yesterday's assignment; clustered standard errors; randomisation inference; CUPED for design; mixture SPRT.

title: A competitor next door
question: What does a competitor's hub next to our site cost?
answer: At AT-0201, a competitor hub opened on 2025-11-29 took about 16% of sessions. Across all 131 openings in the history the loss is 14%.
decision: Price the risk into site choices: a new site next to an existing charger should expect to lose about this share, which the rollout model includes.
rests_on: A synthetic control from 75 motorway high-power sites without a competitor or a price change, matching the site's path before the opening (pre-period error 7.2%).
Placebo test: the gap is larger than at 95% of donor sites where nothing happened (p = 0.05).
Openings fall on dates nobody at EDRI chose, so the network-wide estimate can assume parallel trends.
would_change: A second competitor or a price war nearby, which the placebo sites would not reflect.
method: Synthetic control with an intercept and placebo inference; network-wide imputation estimator with site bootstrap.

title: Energy in the next twelve months
question: How much energy will the existing network sell in the next twelve months?
answer: The existing network will sell about 532 GWh in the next twelve months, +32% on the last twelve.
decision: Plan energy purchasing and grid capacity on this figure; growth slows at the busiest sites as their chargers fill up.
rests_on: Chosen on a backtest of the last twelve months: the capacity-aware site model missed countries by 4.0% a month on average.
seasonal naive with growth: 6.9%.
exponential smoothing: 5.9%.
a gradient-boosted model over all sites: 11.6%.
The 80% intervals come from the backtest's own errors at each horizon.
would_change: New sites or price changes, which this forecast of the existing network at today's prices does not include.
method: Seasonal naive, AutoETS (statsforecast), LightGBM global model (mlforecast), capacity-aware site trends; conformal intervals from a rolling backtest.

title: Where the next 1,000 points go
question: Which sites, and how many points each, for next year's 1,000 high-power points?
answer: Build 107 sites with 1044 points (IT 35, GB 34, DE 29, AT 5, PL 4 sites), for €188m: expected ten-year NPV €514m, and €469m in the worst tenth of scenarios.
decision: Approve this plan. Choosing by traffic alone is expected to earn €171m less; ranking by expected NPV without looking at sites that compete with each other, €23m less.
rests_on: Demand from a Bayesian hierarchical model of 637 established sites (NUTS, r-hat 1.01); unexplained site-to-site variation is 0.45 on the log scale, which is most of the risk.
A nearby charging site costs demand (coefficient -0.14 per unit of proximity); the plan charges for new sites that would compete with each other.
New sites priced like the 2025 increase, with its effect from question 1, and grown with question 4's country growth.
1400 candidates, sizes of 4, 8 or 12 points, within the budget, with at least 18 Italian sites and at most a third of the points in one country.
would_change: A different capex or energy price, which moves sizes before it moves sites.
Grid connection quotes that differ from the planning figures.
method: NumPyro hierarchical model, posterior predictive scenarios, ten-year NPV per scenario, mixed-integer programme with CVaR (HiGHS).
